Aceasta este una dintre cele mai vechi și mai periculoase povești de dragoste…
Afrodita, zeița dragostei, deține o putere fără egal asupra inimii fiecărui zeu și muritor. Deși lumea ei este una a frumuseții, ea este cea mai periculoasă dintre divinități, condusă de pasiune, indiferent de consecințe.

Ares, zeul războiului, e opusul ei: temut, singur, devotat haosului. Ea dă naștere dorinței, el se hrănește din distrugere și ruină.

Însă nici zeii nu sunt feriți de iubire și suferință. Iar dacă zeul războiului este capabil de o iubire mai profundă decât oricine altcineva, atunci și zeița dragostei este capabilă de cele mai cumplite greșeli…

About the author

Jennifer Saint

9 books7,802 followers
Jennifer Saint is a Sunday Times bestselling author. Her debut novel, ARIADNE, was shortlisted for Waterstones Book of the Year 2021 and was a finalist in the Goodreads Choice Awards Fantasy category in 2021. Her second novel, ELEKTRA, comes out in 2022 and is another retelling of Greek mythology told in the voices of the women at the heart of the ancient legends.

Alexia
478 reviews
July 30, 2026
The disappointment I feel from this book is something I believe I will never fully overcome.

I want to focus on the initial 200 pages first. I absolutely loved them; I devoured these pages with enthusiasm, reading quickly and eagerly. I was completely immersed in the story, unable to put the book down.

Aphrodite’s portrayal was as I had envisioned the goddess of love to be: sensual and alluring, yet without an overly sexualized tone. She craved praise and attention, cherishing connections between mortals and immortals alike. Her character embodied a free-spirited, carefree, and mischievous nature, and she took great pleasure in life’s delights. I found myself adoring her.

However, I did have some minor criticisms regarding her demeanor and actions. I thought these issues might be addressed later in the story. Sadly, that expectation was misplaced.

Ares was also depicted in a way that made me swoon. Despite being a formidable god of war, he melted at Aphrodite's feet whenever he was with her. The way this powerful god worshipped and revered her was so romantic that it made me giggle. He respected her deeply, didn't want her to change, and assured her she could have as many lovers as she desired, as long as she returned to him. This level of devotion was such a green flag.

Their relationship felt like a dream come true. I’ve always been more fascinated with the love story between Aphrodite and Ares than that of Persephone and Hades, and this book delivered what I envisioned their relationship to be: passionate and tumultuous.

However, the last 100 pages took a dramatic and negative turn. The narrative shifted from a high point to a surprisingly low one. It changed from a Greek feminist retelling into a Greek retelling told from a woman’s perspective, which is a significant distinction.

Aphrodite's character development stagnated and even regressed rather than progressing. She initially struggled with the reality of war and bloodshed and sought peace, but I had hoped to see her grow and evolve from that mindset. Unfortunately, my hopes were dashed, and my expectations proved too high. It puzzles me why so many authors tend to portray women as opposing violence solely because they are women. Why not write a woman who, despite wishing for peace, also desires war, who isn’t afraid of bloodshed and sometimes enjoys it, who wields power without restraint? I found it perplexing that a goddess like Aphrodite would be depicted this way, especially considering she is the goddess of love, who has the capacity to turn love into something ugly, something capable of causing conflict and war.

Furthermore, the character of Hephaestus also deteriorated as the story progressed. The author attempted to portray him as a gentle, sad god longing for his family’s love, but this approach became excessive, turning into a pity-party tone that felt overdone. She failed to realize that she turned him into a sort of “nice guy,” claiming to support women's empowerment, yet immediately shifting tone when a woman rejected a relationship and preferred friendship instead. His behavior made me profoundly uncomfortable. He kissed Aphrodite without her consent, and the way their marriage was arranged only worsened my disgust. I couldn’t help but laugh when Aphrodite told Hephaestus she preferred to be married to him rather than any other god. In my view, Hephaestus’s character became worse than that of Zeus, Poseidon, and Apollo combined because, unlike those gods who don't hide their true selves, Hephaestus hides behind a facade of kindness, while his true motives remain questionable.

The relationship between Aphrodite and Ares also fell apart entirely, which genuinely hurt me to read. Aphrodite became hypocritical; she never fully understood Ares and constantly wanted to change him, despite his unconditional acceptance and love for her. She failed to recognize that Ares, as the god of war, embodied that identity inherently; it's not just a title but who he is. Similarly, Aphrodite’s identity as the goddess of love is fundamental to her existence. She also refused to see their similarities and how significantly their domains overlapped. Ares was willing to love and accept her without trying to change her, yet Aphrodite never reciprocated to that same extent. Ares truly deserved so much better.

In conclusion, this book will leave a lasting scar because it started so beautifully but ended in complete devastation. The first 200 pages are five-star material, but the last 100 pages drop my rating to just one star.

⭐️ 4 ⭐️ This is a story of a love that can lead to ruin. Aphrodite, the goddess of love, beauty and passion, must learn to choose herself first above all else. In This Immortal Heart, love meets war. Split into five parts, each part focuses on a part of Aphrodites birth, life, love, her forced marriage and the cost of loss and the grief that comes with it. Aphrodite, comes face to face with Ares, the god of war, with whom she begins a love affair that spans mortal lifetimes. She begins to questions the gods' games and her role in the realm. The story highlights how central love is to her, above all else and the novel explores many themes of power vs possession vs freedom.

In part one, we start with her birth and how she is fully grown from the sea foam of the ocean. She is beautiful, powerful and desirable. We see her helping mortals find love and happiness. She takes an interest in Phaon, a human whom she helps find romantic happiness again. Phaon's story eventually connects Aphrodites to Ares, the god of war, as Phaon is caught up in Ares's warfare.

In part two, love and war meet each other and become the emotional core of the novel. Their initial hostility turns into a passionate love affair that gets layered into the political system thats controlled by Zeus. In this portion, we really get to know God of War. He is pain, he is destruction, he is fear. But he is not short of love and tenderness. Through his relationship to Aphrodites we learn that he can be nurturing, kind, protective. Their attraction really works here because Aphrodites is someone who understands connection and desires and Ares is someone who understands power and circumstances. Together, opposites attract and it was so beautiful seeing their relationship unfold.

In part three and four, the novel turns more political. We meet Zeus, Hera, Hephaestus and Adonis. There is a conflict between Hera and Zeus, resulting in Hephaestus being cast out. He retaliates, casting more destruction in the wake of his actions, which involves Aphrodites to become at odds with her heart vs duty. We get to see a different side of Aphrodite's here, a more distraught, sadder, emotionally diminished. There were choices made in this part of the novel that did not sit well with me but I understood why they had to be written in such a way to deliver the next part of the story. While written beautifully, this was my least favorite part of the narrative. This part hurt, be prepared!

In final part of the novel, following several years later, Aphrodite finds Ares living among the Amazonians in Scythia. Changed by the years of the past, they are now different people. Their reconciliation is bittersweet. And the ending suggests that it's not a simple reunion but rather one that shows that two opposite forces can coexist with each other. Despite the anger, pain and emotional suffering, our immortal hearts will always be connected by passion, vulnerability and recognizing/accepting the domains that others possess.

As someone who has a deep appreciation of Greek mythology but isn't well versed in it, I found this story striking for how it highlighted more gentler qualities of Ares and Aphrodite. I've read some books where Aphrodites came across as harsh and vain, but Saints given her a softer moral compass with humane qualities that really resonated with the embodiment of beauty, passion and love. The relationship between Ares and Aphrodites made me stop and think about the qualities that draw us to other (polar opposite) people. In order to understand love, I think we have to embrace and endure everything that comes with it.



Many thanks to NetGalley, Ballentine Publisher and the author, Jennifer Saint for an early copy.

Publication date: June 9, 2026

January 1, 2026
Jennifer Saint offers an ambitious reimagining of one of Greek mythology’s most complex goddesses, but ultimately This Immortal Heart feels uneven in its execution. While there are moments of insight, the narrative arc struggles to build tension or fully explore the implications of its own creative choices.

One of the strongest aspects of the novel is the characterisation of Aphrodite herself. Saint presents her as thoughtful and observant, and there are glimpses of a more introspective goddess beneath the familiar veneer of beauty and desire. However, Aphrodite often feels frustratingly passive. Despite being positioned as a powerful, ancient deity, she frequently reacts to events rather than shaping them, which undercuts the authority and agency the narrative seems to promise. This passivity is especially noticeable in her relationship with Ares. Ares feels underdeveloped, and the emotional foundation of their relationship feels thin. There is not enough build-up to make their connection compelling, which weakens what should be one of the most dynamic and charged relationships in Greek myth.

The retelling itself is extremely loose, and while reinterpretation is expected, the degree of deviation here often diminishes the story’s stakes. The marriage narrative is significantly altered, along with Hephaestus’s character. Galatea fleeing to Artemis’ forests and becoming her lover feels trite. Moreover, Eros is already born and has no father, rather than being fathered by Ares. These choices feel arbitrary rather than purposeful. Because the story selectively reshapes mythological elements without fully committing to the consequences of those changes, it becomes difficult to feel any real tension. The plot seems to pick and choose which myths to honour based on convenience, rather than using them to build a coherent internal logic.

The decision to make Aphrodite the daughter of Ouranos rather than Zeus is one of the more intriguing decisions, but it is not explored deeply enough. This origin should give Aphrodite a vastly different perspective from the Olympians—particularly given her references to being older than Ares and other gods. However, the calamity of her birth feels more like an afterthought than a defining aspect of her character. It rarely informs her decision-making or worldview in a meaningful way. Instead of delving into this unique perspective, the novel often falls back on extended sequences of plotting and name-dropping minor mythological figures—what readers have come to expect from Greek myth retellings, but without enough variation or emotional payoff to make them feel fresh. Without stronger character-driven tension or clearer thematic focus, these sections begin to feel repetitive.

Overall, while the novel has an interesting premise and a solid central character, it lacks narrative tension and emotional stakes. The looseness of the retelling, combined with underdeveloped relationships and missed opportunities for deeper character exploration, prevents the arc from fully realising its potential.

I received an advance review copy for free via NetGalley. I am leaving this review voluntarily 📚.

These last few months have been incredibly chaotic and honestly put me into such a reading slump, but oh my gosh… this book gave me everything I needed 😭

I surprisingly took my time reading this one and savoured every word. It was such a beautifully written and entertaining story. The romance felt gentle and fresh, and I adored every minute spent with Aphrodite and Ares together.

Of course, like all of Jennifer Saint's retellings, I really appreciated the feminist perspective woven throughout the story. The pacing was also perfect for me, and while the writing is simple, it still felt lush and captivating.

I will say I was not quite as invested in Part 3 or the larger conflicts between the gods. The love story was by far my favourite aspect, and honestly, I wish it had been even more of the focal point.

Overall though, this felt like such a lovely breath of fresh air, and I would definitely recommend!

This is a really difficult one for me to rate as I genuinely think my own personal rating will differ from the majority of readers so take that with a grain of salt.

I took a good chunk of time off of mythology retellings after the craze took off and Madeline Miller did her thing. We saw an influx of retellings and while part of me loves that because I LOVE mythology, there was a lot of trash in the mix as everyone put out what they could as fast as they were able.

Years ago, I read Ariadne and it was one of the last retellings I recall reading. I felt like it was average as well and decided I should take some time off the genre and really be picky going forward. Years later, I figured I would give This Immortal Heart a try aa Aphrodite is weirdly so beloved and yet largely unexplored. But this also just fell so short for me and I’m questioning a lot of the tone, voice, and style that is going into retellings nowadays more than anything else.

It’s not that this book is inherently bad by any means, but it does read more as YA. Of course there are going to be some more “adult” and heavier subjects but I’ve read a lot of YA that tonally handles themes and subjects in a harsher light that makes it more adult. But I felt the tone and plot was so lackluster and quite frankly, juvenile. I’m not sure if I’m the only one that’s been feeling this way but it truly read like an average romantasy protagonist and not the actual goddess Aphrodite. She could’ve been anyone and it made reading and connecting the mythos I’m so in love with impossible. And this is not to say I’m shitting on romantasy or any other genre as there’s gold intermingled everywhere. But I just truly couldn’t read this as a mythos retelling and to me, isn’t that the whole point?

I love Jennifer Saint's Greek retellings, they're very accessible and easy to read. This time she takes on the story of Aphrodite and her tumultuous relationship with Ares, the God of War. It's interspersed with some stories of the mortals who Aphrodite influences along the way - from Galatea to Phaon and the Amazonians. It also explores her rather complicated relationship with Hephaestus, and her place amongst the Olympians.

Aphrodite has always held an interesting place on Mt Olympus, not one of the siblings of Zeus but set apart, with a power that transcends Gods and mortals alike. It was fun to see her weave her influence and explore a softer side to her character. Too often Aphrodite is perceived as superficial and simpering to the Gods. Not so here.

I think this would be a good starting novel for those dipping their toes in Greek myth retellings, as Saint manages to bring these characters to life without overwhelming the reader in lore. There's some fun Easter eggs for avid Greek myth lovers, but prior knowledge isn't necessary to enjoy this. Fun time.

Well, this is it—the final book from this author, and to be honest, I am ready for a change of pace. Electra has been my favourite out of all the novels, and in my opinion, it was really well written. This one, however, I found a bit hit-and-miss.

Aphrodite is a very different breed of goddess than Hera. She plays a very wily game to keep the other male gods at bay and remain unmarried. She has many lovers in this book (which I am not overly keen on!) but staying unwed and un-Zeus'ed is quite an achievement, frankly. Even his own sisters didn’t manage that at times! Except, of course, for the MVP GOAT that is Hestia.

I was glad to see that Aphrodite was kind to Hephaestus in this book. He and Hestia are probably some of my favourite characters on Mount Olympus.

Note: I was a bit surprised that the author chose to vary some of her myths even between her own books, but that is actually quite true to real Greek mythology, so I wasn't too upset about it.

The casual sex was frequent, and I just did not enjoy that. It is Aphrodite, though, so I am trying to get past it, but I just do not want to read about it. By about halfway through, I found myself skimming. To be honest, I'm just not really feeling this author anymore. I'm glad this is the last one in her bibliography because I want something new.

That said, the part where Aphrodite becomes Hephaestus' wife is really well written. Ares disappearing after Aphrodite agrees to the promise to marry Hephaestus, and love in the world going off course because Aphrodite is heartbroken—it’s all skilfully done. Aphrodite's relationships with Eros and Demeter are also very sweet.

I think the issue with this book, as well as with Hera, is the long lifespan of the characters. It makes everything seem a bit pointless. Lots of mortals die, and it all kind of means nothing in the end. It feels very episodic, which works well in standalone myths but doesn't work for me as a cohesive book.

I think what should have happened here was for the author to pick a few myths centred on, say, Ares and Aphrodite, and focus completely on them. Nobody cares about Adonis or Aphrodite's trips to other lovers. It dilutes the plot and makes for a more drawn-out, weaker story. I wanted to see Ares and Aphrodite's story exclusively. The beginning of the book was quite strong but right now I am just glad that it is over.

P.S. This was not the Kevin Smith Ares that I had in my head. Disappointed 💔

"A god who thrives on chaos... whose wildness can be tamed only by me."
Wow I really loved this. I've enjoyed JS's past novels but this is easily her best, in my opinion. It definitely has a more upbeat and hopeful tone- this is the goddess of love, after all- and leans into the romance, which as a romance reader I personally loved.

The depictions of both Aphrodite and Ares were refreshing, in my opinion. So often Aphrodite is shown as self-absorbed and fickle, often using her gift of love to play with those around her. Here we see a goddess who just loves love. She genuinely cares about her followers and wants to make the world a better place, with as much love as possible in it. She tries to keep the peace on Olympus and ease the discord between the other gods and goddesses, while also caring about the mortals they reign over.

Ares too had a depth to him- he's not a raging hot-head who's only care is violence. He goes to war because that's just who he is- he can't stop it any more than Aphrodite can stop being the goddess of love. He acknowledges the ugliness in it and concedes maybe one day, war will cease to exist.

I adored the romance between these two. The myths of their affair are of course famous- but here it had such longing and angst. I loved the scenes we got of Ares looking out for Aphrodite and returning to Mount Olympus again and again for her. He was so soft and different with her, which as she knows is a side that only she ever got to see.

I have read every single one of Jennifer Saint’s books, so This Immortal Heart was immediately on my order list the moment it was released. And honestly… I think this might be my favorite one yet. That might also be because Aphrodite is my favorite goddess, but still.

This book honestly felt like stepping into a dream. The way love and passion are described as all-consuming, the way Aphrodite deeply loves her realm and does everything she can for her worshippers. It was just beautiful to read. And what I really appreciated is that she isn’t perfect. She makes mistakes, she doesn’t always foresee how her gifts will play out, and that only makes her more relatable. What matters is that she always tries to make things right again, like with Galatea’s story.

Beyond the usual messy Olympian family dynamics, this book really felt like an ode to love in all its forms.

Aphrodite’s own love story shows so clearly that love and heartbreak can happen to anyone, even the goddess of love herself. But what I loved most is how she handles that heartbreak. She allows herself to feel it, to heal, and then she rises again. She remembers who she is. She doesn’t stay stuck in sadness, she finds her power again, her joy, and uses that not just to save herself, but to bring love back into the world for others too.

This book was poetic, whimsical, empowering, and honestly just felt magical. Like being wrapped up in a dream.

I have read negative reviews that said that after 200 pages the book got dull and boring, but to me it only got better the further I went into the story. I'm truly obsessed with this book if you couldn't tell yet.

I absolutely loved this newest addition to Saint’s work. And I'm so so curious to see who will be the next character that Jennifer Saint will write about. I will be ready to buy it for sure.

Five stars, without a doubt.

Jennifer Saint has built her career on giving the women of Greek mythology room to breathe outside the narrow frames their original poets gave them. With This Immortal Heart by Jennifer Saint, she steps onto unfamiliar ground in two ways at once. First, she hands the narration to a goddess rather than a mortal woman. Second, she leans openly into romance for the first time, threading her usual mythological scholarship through the bones of a love story that her acknowledgements freely admit is her switch into the genre.

The result is a sensuous, slow-burning retelling of Aphrodite and Ares, an affair the ancient sources usually treated as gossip, scandal, or a punchline involving Hephaestus and a golden net. Saint takes that tabloid sliver and stretches it across centuries.

Premise and Setup, Spoiler-Free

Aphrodite tells her own story. She is newly born from sea-foam and her father's blood, comfortable in her power, devoted to her worshippers' secrets and the quiet pleasures she stirs in mortal and divine hearts alike. Her dalliances are brief and bright, and she is determined never to marry, having watched what marriage has done to Hera.

Then a battle she cannot prevent steals away a mortal she has just blessed with a second chance. The man behind the spear is Ares, brooding, untouchable, despised by most of Olympus. Their spheres of power could not be more opposed: she stirs longing, he stirs war. Beneath the friction, the two recognise something of themselves in each other. What follows is a courtship pulled taut between desire, divine politics, and the bargains gods are forced to make in Zeus's court.

The Voice in This Book

Saint writes Aphrodite in a register that feels deliberately drawn from her source material:

A languorous, sensory prose style indebted to Sappho and Ovid
Long looping sentences thick with petals, oils, salt, smoke, and skin
A first-person narrator who is amused, observant, slightly vain, and not above admitting it
Cool, quick dialogue that offsets the lyrical interior monologue

Readers who came to her through Hera, Atalanta, Elektra, or Ariadne will recognise her instinct for plain emotional clarity inside ornate sentences. But Aphrodite is a different kind of narrator. She is a goddess speaking in her prime, not a girl looking back on a tragedy, and the book takes its tonal cues from her appetite for the world.

What the Book Does Well

A few craft choices come through as genuinely strong:

The mortal interludes. Phaon, Pygmalion's Galatea, Pandora, Iphis, and Adonis each anchor a self-contained novella in miniature stitched into the larger arc, and they carry much of the book's moral weight.
The reframing of familiar episodes. Hephaestus's exile, Pandora's jar, the trial at the Areopagus. Saint diverges from the versions she used in her earlier novel Hera, and the author's note is refreshingly honest about why.
The chemistry. Ares is written with restraint rather than posturing. He listens before he speaks, and the slow accumulation of his presence in Aphrodite's thoughts is one of the book's best-paced threads.
The Amazons sequence. The detour to Scythia, drawn from Adrienne Mayor's nonfiction work, gives the second half fresh geographic and emotional air.
Where the Cracks Show

For a romance promising sparks between fire and passion, the early courtship sometimes runs cooler than the blurb suggests. Saint's lyrical instincts occasionally smother the heat she is supposed to be generating, and a few central encounters are described with so much atmospheric language that the bodies and stakes inside them go a little soft.

Other readers may stumble on these points:

Aphrodite's mortal lovers in the first hundred pages can blur into one another, since they share a rhythm of meeting, melting, and moving on.
The Olympian council scenes carry useful exposition but slow the pulse whenever they appear back to back.
Hephaestus, who carries enormous narrative weight, is granted less interiority than the central pair, which makes one major turn in part two feel more engineered than inevitable.
The mortal subplots are sometimes so vivid that the central romance suffers by comparison.

None of these are fatal flaws, but they explain why the book reads, even to admirers, as a strong four-out-of-five rather than a clear five.

Where This Sits in Saint's Wider Work

This Immortal Heart by Jennifer Saint is her fifth novel. Ariadne was the breakout, Elektra and Atalanta both hit number one on the Sunday Times list, and Hera reframed the queen of Olympus through her grievances and her dignity. Set against those, this is the warmest book she has written. Less brutal than Elektra, less wounded than Ariadne, less politically claustrophobic than Hera. It is the book of an author granting herself permission to enjoy her gods.

It is also the first of her novels where the protagonist openly wants pleasure, and where the page lingers on it without flinching. For longtime readers, that loosening of register is the most interesting evolution on offer.

Who Will Love It

Anyone expecting a fast paranormal romance in togas may need to recalibrate. This is mythology first, romance second. It is best suited for:

Readers who loved Madeline Miller's Circe and want a similarly reflective, first-person goddess voice
Fans of Natalie Haynes who enjoy mythological retellings with a feminist edge
Romance readers willing to trade urgency for atmosphere
Anyone who has wanted Saint to give the gods themselves the microphone

If you prefer the tighter dread of Ariadne or the white-hot vengeance of Elektra, you may find this softer at the edges. That softness is, I think, part of its argument.

Closing Thoughts

This Immortal Heart by Jennifer Saint is not a flawless novel, but it is a confident one. Saint knows what her readers come to her for, and she gives them that while also taking a real risk in opening the door to romance. The book glows more than it burns, ruminates more than it races, and makes a quietly radical case inside its mythological frame: love is not weaker than war, it just outlasts it. For readers willing to sit inside that argument, This Immortal Heart by Jennifer Saint is a generous, lyrical addition to her body of work, and a promising opening if she chooses to write more in this register.
